rationale:
The tests adequately cover `requirements.sdk.graph.search.StructuralMatch`. I judged this from the supplied test source and did not request implementation source.

Obligations derived from the text:
1. The type has public `node: OutlineData` and `excerpt: String` fields, and `StructuralMatch::new(node, excerpt)` builds a value from them.
2. `node` identifies the enclosing outline item of a match.
3. `excerpt` is the text of the matched byte range, which may be smaller than the enclosing item.

Coverage:
- Construction and field contents: `crates/trust-but-verify/tests/search.rs#fn[callers_can_construct_complete_and_partial_search_results]` is an external-crate test. It calls `StructuralMatch::new(address.clone(), "example".into())`, which works despite `#[non_exhaustive]`. It then asserts `matches[0].node == address` and `matches[0].excerpt == "example"`, which covers the public fields and the constructor.
- Enclosing node and sub-item excerpt, built-in provider: `crates/trust-but-verify/tests/source_defaults.rs#fn[built_in_languages_and_structural_search_use_the_project_scope]` searches real Rust files for the pattern `call()`. The match sits inside `fn visible() { call(); }`. The test asserts `node.path == visible.rs` and `node.selector == "fn[visible]"`, so `node` is the enclosing function. It asserts `excerpt == "call()"`, so the excerpt is the matched range and is smaller than the enclosing item. It also checks the Python language case on the path.
- Enclosing node and sub-item excerpt, overridden provider: `crates/trust-but-verify/src/sources/tests.rs#fn[structural_search_uses_overridden_parses_their_snapshot_and_requested_scope]` asserts `node.path`, `node.selector == "fn[cached]"` and `excerpt == "call()"` for each match the provider returns.
- Export inventory: `crates/trust-but-verify/tests/public_api.rs#fn[public_exports_match_the_appendix]` checks that the public API matches the documented inventory.

The requirement does not define behavior for nested enclosing items or multibyte excerpts, so I treated those as unspecified rather than as gaps. I found no requirement-violating behavior that these tests would accept.
